paper_title: HINT-WAM: Hindsight-Informed Training for World Action Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: World action models (WAMs) have shown promising generalization and data efficiency in robot manipulation by coupling action generation with predictions of future visual dynamics. Translating these capabilities into reliable task execution, however, remains a challenge for existing post-training methods. Offline supervised fine-tuning provides dense supervision on expert trajectories, but its flow-matching action expert is trained only on noised demonstration actions and never on the intermediate states produced by its own sampler; task-specific adaptation can also compromise pretrained capabilities. On-policy reinforcement learning trains on the policy's own behavior, yet sparse task rewards make exploration and credit assignment difficult, while dense reward shaping still provides scalar evaluations rather than direct action targets. We introduce \textbf{HINT-WAM}, the first on-policy self-distillation framework that supervises the action expert on its own sampling trajectories using hindsight, the future video of the demonstration, as privileged information available to the WAM itself. For each demonstration observation, the student generates its action through its own denoising trajectory, and at the states along this trajectory the same model acts as a teacher conditioned additionally on this hindsight, providing a conditional action distribution as a dense training target, while the student sees only deployment-time inputs and needs no environmental rewards or simulator interaction. To transfer this supervision to a flow-matching action expert, HINT-WAM distills the teacher into the student with an energy score, a distribution-level objective that matches the teacher's action distribution from the student's own samples rather than regressing its velocity field. The project web is available in https://tuandattt.github.io/hintwam/.

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: World action models (WAMs) have shown promising generalization and data efficiency in robot manipulation by coupling action generation with predictions of future visual dynamics. Translating these capabilities into reliable task execution, however, remains challenge for existing post-training methods. Offline supervised fine-tuning provides dense supervision on expert trajectories, but its flowmatching action expert is trained only on noised demonstration actions and never on the intermediate states produced by its own sampler; task-specific adaptation can also compromise pretrained capabilities. On-policy reinforcement learning trains on the policys own behavior, yet sparse task rewards make exploration and credit assignment difficult, while dense reward shaping still provides scalar evaluations rather than direct action targets. We introduce HINT-WAM, the first on-policy self-distillation framework that supervises the action expert on its own sampling trajectories using hindsight, the future video of the demonstration, as privileged information available to the WAM itself. For each demonstration observation, the student generates its action through its own denoising trajectory, and at the states along this trajectory the same model acts as teacher conditioned additionally on this hindsight, providing conditional action distribution as dense training target, while the student sees only deployment-time inputs and needs no environmental rewards or simulator interaction. The project web is available in this link. 1. Introduction World action models (WAMs) have demonstrated promising generalization and data efficiency for robot manipulation by coupling action generation with future visual prediction [17, 21, 49]. Recent models generate continuous action chunks through flow matching, providing an expressive interface between visual predictions and robot motion [2, 21]. Despite this progress, reliable execution on downstream tasks [22, 23] still requires adaptation to task-specific demands and to the deviations that arise during closed-loop interaction. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) offers straightforward adaptation strategy by providing dense action targets from expert demonstrations. However, SFT supervises the model only on demonstration data. During training, the action expert sees only noised versions of the ground-truth actions and never the intermediate states produced by its own sampler, form of exposure bias [33] and the sampler-level counterpart of the compounding errors at deployment [38], whose environment-level gap requires closed-loop interaction. Moreover, given only the current observation, demonstrated action chunk is one of several plausible continuations, and the SFT target does not reveal which one the demonstrator followed. Finally, adapting pretrained model to narrow task distribution can degrade previously acquired capabilities [40]. On-policy reinforcement learning (RL) addresses the state-distribution mismatch by optimizing the policy on its own rollouts, motivating its use in VLA and WAM posttraining [20, 32, 36]. However, many manipulation tasks offer only sparse success rewards, making exploration and credit assignment costly when successful trajectories are rarely sampled. Even with denser, reconstruction-based rewards [36], reward-based optimization only evaluates sampled behavior through scalar feedback, leaving the policy to infer how its actions should change. This motivates supplying structured action supervision directly on the states produced by the policys own action sampler. Our key insight is that the future frames of demonstration, which we call hindsight, carry privileged information about the intended task progression, connecting learning with privileged information [8, 43] to on-policy distillation [1]. We build on this insight in HINT-WAM: the same model serves as teacher that additionally reads the hindsight, whereas the student observes only the inputs available at deployment and is supervised on the states produced by its own action sampler. Throughout this paper, on-policy refers to the generation of actions: as in on-policy distillation for language models [1], where prompts are drawn from dataset and the student generates the response, observations are drawn from demonstrations and the student generates the denoising trajectory of its action chunk. We do not collect new environment states. Transferring this supervision to flow-matching action expert introduces further challenge. Such experts generate continuous actions by integrating velocity field, so the token-level probability matching used in autoregressive distillation does not apply directly. Regressing the teachers velocity field would drive the student toward the teachers conditional mean, which averages over modes that the student cannot distinguish without hindsight. We therefore distill the teacher with the energy score [14], strictly proper scoring rule that matches the teachers action distribution from the students own samples and one teacher sample. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We introduce HINT-WAM, self-distillation framework for world action models in which the policy acts as its own teacher given hindsight, requiring neither separately trained teacher nor environmental rewards or simulator interaction. We propose distribution-level distillation objective for flow-matching action experts based on the energy score, which avoids the mode averaging of velocity regression and requires no action-likelihood evaluation. The framework adapts the action expert while keeping the worldmodeling backbone frozen. Comprehensive experiments on LIBERO-90 and RoboTwin 2.0 demonstrate that HINT-WAM consistently improves post-training performance over SFT and matched baselines, while mitigating the catastrophic forgetting of pretrained skills. 2. Related Work 2.1. World Action Models Vision-language-action (VLA) models combine large-scale multimodal pretraining with diverse robot demonstrations to translate camera observations and language instructions into robot commands [6, 18, 34, 50]. Rather than discretizing actions into tokens, many recent policies generate continuous action chunks with diffusion [10] or flow matching [5, 27]. World action models (WAMs) additionally reason about how the scene will evolve [39], and differ mainly in how tightly they tie prediction to control. Some extract predictive visual representations from video model to condition separate action head [17], while others generate future frames and actions jointly through shared denoising process or unified video action backbone [16, 25, 49]. Autoregressive designs such as LingBot-VA interleave video and action prediction for closed-loop control [21], and RoboDreamer exploits imagined dynamics for planning [48]. Recent architectures pair large world-modeling backbone with lightweight flowmatching action expert [2]. While these works study WAM design and pretraining, HINT-WAM post-trains only the action expert on the states the policy visits. 2.2. On-Policy Self-Distillation On-policy distillation builds on the observation, first formalized by DAgger [38], that policy learns most effectively from the states it reaches on its own rather than from those recorded by demonstrator. GKD [1] and MiniLLM [15] adopt this principle for compressing large language models: the student generates its own sequences, which the teacher then scores token by token, and MiniLLM additionally argues for the mode-seeking reverse KL as the distillation objective. more recent line of work removes the need for separate, larger teacher by letting single model play both roles, where the teacher is the model itself given privileged information that the student does not see. Self-Distilled Reasoner [47] trains reasoning model on its own on-policy samples under the supervision of copy conditioned on reference solutions, dOPSD [11] extends this self-distillation scheme to diffusion language models, and PRISM [12] applies it to the design of communication topologies in multi-agent systems, guiding the designer with privileged sibling. All of these methods operate on discrete tokens and rely on likelihood-based objectives. HINT-WAM brings on-policy self-distillation to embodied control, where the student is flow-matching action expert that generates continuous actions without tractable likelihood. Unlike prior flow-matching distillation methods, which regress the teachers velocity field [13, 24], we match action distributions with proper scoring rule, the energy score [14], which needs only one teacher sample per state. 2.3. On-Policy Distillation for World Action Models Recent works bring on-policy distillation to WAMs, supervising the student on its own rollouts with separate, stronger task-specific teacher, either through joint video action targets [44] or by replaying fixed pool of student and teacher trajectories [29]. The former queries the teacher for paired video and action targets on student rollout histories, while the latter reweights each replayed decision with prefix-based importance weights to correct the shift between stored and current histories. These methods require an additional teacher model, making post-training computationally expensive. In contrast, HINT-WAM derives the teacher from the student itself by adding only lightweight hindsight branch. To the best of our knowledge, it is the first self-distillation framework for world action models. 3. Method This section presents HINT-WAM, which post-trains pretrained WAM by letting the model act as its own teacher given hindsight. We first review the base model (Sec. 3.1) and outline the framework (Sec. 3.2), then describe the hindsight teacher (Sec. 3.3) and its distillation into the student (Sec. 3.4). 3.1. Preliminaries Base world action model. We build on Fast-WAM [45], world action model whose backbone is Mixture-ofTransformers [26] with two experts that share single attention operation in every layer. The video expert is large pretrained video diffusion transformer [42] operating on video VAE latents, and the action expert is lightweight diffusion transformer that generates an action chunk RHD of control steps. The policy is conditioned on an observation = (I, ℓ, s) consisting of the current camera frame I, the language instruction ℓ, and the proprioceptive state s. Overview Standard SFT minimizes Eq. (1) on the demonstrations and therefore suffers from exposure bias and target ambiguity (Sec. 1). Following on-policy self-distillation for language models [47], we let single network serve as both teacher and student, where the teacher additionally receives hindsight [4]: the future video of the demonstration. Hindsight is available in every demonstration at no extra cost and resolves the ambiguity of the SFT target, while distilling on the students own sampling trajectories addresses the exposure bias. As shown in Fig. 2, HINT-WAM proceeds in three stages: Stage 0 (SFT). The action expert is fine-tuned on the demonstrations with Eq. (1), giving the student initialization θ0. Stage (hindsight teacher). With θ0 frozen, lightweight hindsight encoder and gated adapters learn to read the future video, giving the teacher = (θ0, ψ). Stage (on-policy self-distillation). The student θ, initialized from θ0, is trained to match the teacher on its own sampling trajectories, with only the action expert updated. The video expert stays frozen in every stage. At deployment, only the student is used, so the policy never requires access to the future. 3.3. We post-train on its 3,921 demonstrations and evaluate each task with 50 trials from the fixed initial states of LIBERO. To measure forgetting, we additionally evaluate the 40 tasks of the four original suites, which also provide small replay memory for our continual variant. RoboTwin 2.0 covers dual-arm manipulation over 50 tasks. Since the released checkpoint was trained on these tasks, we evaluate on hard subset of 25 tasks, selected before any training, with 50 episodes each in the clean and randomized settings. All methods share the same initial states, number of trials, and sampler. Training details. We keep the architecture and sampler of the released Fast-WAM checkpoints unchanged, with 32-step action chunks generated by 10 Euler steps. The hindsight encoder and the adapters add about 13M parameters (0.2%), used only by the teacher. All stages use AdamW [31] with cosine schedule and an effective batch size of 192 on 8 A5000 GPUs. Comparison Results We compare HINT-WAM with the following baselines, which share its starting checkpoint, data, trainable parameters, optimizer, and training budget unless stated otherwise: Fast-WAM [45]: the released checkpoint. SFT: fine-tunes the action expert with Eq. (1), without teacher or on-policy states. Full SFT: fine-tunes both the video and action experts. BC control: continues SFT with the BC loss only (λdist = 0), testing the effect of additional training. Self-imitation: adds successful rollouts of the SFT policy from randomized placements to the demonstrations and trains with behavior cloning. Shuffled hindsight: runs HINT-WAM, but the teacher reads the future of another episode, removing only the privileged information. On RoboTwin, we compare with Fast-WAM, full SFT, and the BC control. Results on LIBERO-90. As shown in Tab. 1, the released Fast-WAM checkpoint solves only small fraction of the unseen LIBERO-90 tasks, and SFT raises its success rate to 78.88%. HINT-WAM further improves it to 85.18%, gain of 6.30% over SFT on average across the 90 tasks (paired = 3.58). It also surpasses full SFT, which finetunes both experts, by 3.94% while training only the action expert. The comparison baselines show where this gain comes from. First, it does not stem from additional training: continuing SFT with the same number of steps but without the teacher lowers the success rate to 71.56%. Second, it does not stem from training on the policys own data alone: adding the policys successful rollouts improves SFT by only 0.74%, and HINT-WAM outperforms self-imitation by 5.56% (paired = 2.96). Third, the gain is carried by the privileged information: when the teacher reads the future of another episode, the identical pipeline reaches only 80.28%, 4.90% below HINT-WAM (paired = 2.76). On RoboTwin 2.0, the released checkpoint was already trained on the same demonstrations, which leaves little headroom. Continued behavior cloning lowers success in both the clean and the randomized settings, by 1.12% and 1.36%, and full SFT also falls below the released checkpoint. In contrast, HINT-WAM stays at or slightly above the released checkpoint and outperforms the BC control by 1.68% in the clean setting (paired = 2.00) and by 1.60% in the randomized setting. The gains are smaller than on LIBERO-90 but show the same trend: given the same training budget, hindsight distillation improves the policy where additional imitation degrades it. 4.3. Continual Learning Results Without replay. As shown in Tab. 2, post-training on LIBERO-90 alone causes severe forgetting on the four original suites for every method, reducing their average success from 96.55% to below 45%. HINT-WAM retains the most (44.05%, vs. 37.45% for SFT), while full SFT forgets the most (32.85%): updating the video expert as well helps on the new tasks but erodes considerably more of the pretrained skills. Distilled on its own sampling trajectories, the student stays closer to its current behavior than under offpolicy imitation, reducing but not preventing forgetting. With replay. Experience replay largely closes the gap, and HINT-WAM composes with it. With replay, HINTWAM outperforms SFT by 4.86% on the new tasks (paired = 2.66) and by 3.55% on the original suites, coming within 1.5% of the released checkpoint, with the largest gain on the long-horizon suite (9.0%). It also leads full SFT by 3.92% and 2.20%, respectively, showing that hindsight distillation is complementary to replay. 4.4. Computational Cost Fig. 3 separates the effect of HINT-WAM from that of additional training. SFT has converged: training from 3,000 to 5,000 steps costs 22 more hours and leaves success unchanged, and spending the same steps on BC lowers success, suggesting that further imitation overfits. Ablation Study Distribution matching. Fig. 4 compares four distillation objectives under the same teacher, on-policy states, anchor, , and training budget. Velocity matching reaches 79.02%, essentially SFT (+0.14%, paired = 0.09), as regressing the teachers velocity drives the student toward its conditional mean. Kernel Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) between the student samples and the teacher sample reaches 80.63%: although it matches distributions in principle, its Gaussian-kernel gradients vanish once samples lie farther apart than the bandwidth, as is common for high-dimensional action chunks. Action-space MSE on the implied actions reaches 82.93%, but it is minimized by collapsing every student sample onto the teachers mean, which discards the teachers uncertainty and conflicts with the flow-matching anchor; its gradient also grows with distance, so single noisy teacher sample can dominate. The energy score, which is MMD with the distance kernel, avoids both issues: it matches the full distribution, needs no bandwidth, and has unit-norm gradients at every distance. It reaches 85.18%, 6.16% above velocity matching (paired = 3.62, 48 wins vs. 17 losses, sign-test = 0.0004). Behavior-cloning anchor. Fig. 5 shows that neither ingredient helps on its own. Continued imitation lowers success from 78.9% to 71.6%, and distillation without the anchor falls to 74.4%, below its own SFT initialization, since nothing ties the student to the demonstrations and errors of the teacher and of its own sampling can accumulate. Combined, the two reach 85.2%: while they change success by 7.3% and 4.5% alone, together they add +6.3%, strong interaction rather than two additive effects. The anchor thus keeps the student on the demonstration distribution, while distillation corrects it on the states it visits. Number of student samples. Fig. 6 varies the number of student samples in Eq. (8). With = 1, the repulsion term vanishes, yet the variant still reaches 81.4% and outperforms velocity matching. Adding samples improves success monotonically to 85.2% at = 4, by 1.11.4% per sample. Action-space MSE with = 4, which also lacks repulsion, reaches only 82.9%, so the gain at = 4 stems from the repulsion that preserves the diversity of the students samples rather than from the number of samples alone. Since the curve has not saturated, larger may help further, at one more gradient-free rollout per sample. On-policy states. Fig. 7 isolates where the student is supervised. Replacing the students sampler states with demonstrated actions noised to the same points σk, i.e., the states seen by SFT, reaches only 80.7%, whereas the students own sampling trajectories reach 85.2%. The shuffled-hindsight baseline (80.3%, Tab. 1), which keeps on-policy states but removes the privileged information, shows the converse. Hindsight and on-policy states thus each improve SFT by less than 2% alone but add 6.3% together: the teachers correction is most useful on the denoising states the student actually reaches at inference. 5. Conclusion We presented HINT-WAM, the first on-policy selfdistillation framework for world action models, in which hindsight teacher sharing the students backbone supervises the action expert on its own sampler states with the energy score. Without an external teacher, rewards, or simulator, HINT-WAM outperforms SFT on LIBERO-90 and RoboTwin 2.0, forgets less, and composes with replay. Since its on-policy states come from the sampler rather than closed-loop interaction, closed-loop data collection is natural next step.

sections.title: Supplementary Material
sections.content: This supplementary material provides additional details and results for HINT-WAM. Sec. describes the implementation and hyperparameters, Sec. the training cost, Sec. the checks of the hindsight teacher, Sec. the full paired statistics on LIBERO-90, Sec. per-task analysis, Sec. further RoboTwin 2.0 results, Sec. the LIBERO90 evaluation protocol, Sec. the self-imitation baseline, Sec. the selection of the objective and learning rate, Sec. toy experiment on mode averaging, Sec. qualitative rollouts, and Sec. discussion of the main design questions. A. Implementation Details and Hyperparameters Datasets. For LIBERO-90, we use the LeRobot-format release of the 90 tasks, comprising 3,921 demonstrations and 569K frames recorded at 20 Hz. The policy observes an agent-view and wrist camera at 224 224, concatenated horizontally into single frame, and predicts 7-D actions (end-effector pose deltas and gripper). Forgetting is measured on the 40 tasks of the four original LIBERO suites (Spatial, Object, Goal, and Long) with 50 trials each. For the continual variant, the replay memory contains 5 demonstrations per original task (200 episodes) sampled once with fixed seed; repeated four times, it accounts for about 19% of the training frames and is mixed into every training stage. On RoboTwin 2.0, the policy observes head camera and two wrist cameras at 384 320 and predicts 14-D actions (joint positions and grippers of both arms). We train on the demonstrations of the 50 tasks used by the released checkpoint and hold out 1% of the episodes. All methods use the normalization statistics of the released checkpoints. Architecture. The Mixture-of-Transformers backbone of Fast-WAM has 30 layers. Its video expert is the Wan2.2TI2V-5B diffusion transformer (5.00B parameters), and its action expert is diffusion transformer with 1.02B parameters. Each action chunk spans = 32 control steps, and the video window covers 33 frames, of which every fourth frame is encoded by the VAE. Actions are generated with 10 Euler steps on schedule with shift 5, both during training and at inference. Our modules are used only by the teacher. The hindsight encoder takes the VAE latents of the future frames, dropping the first latent frame, mean-pools them over space, and applies linear layer (48 512) followed by LayerNorm. Eight learned queries then pool the sequence with 8-head attention, followed by linear layer and LayerNorm, so that ϕ R8512. The gated adapters are attached after layers {4, 9, 14, 19, 24, 29} of the action expert with bottleneck width of 512 and 8 heads, and are initialized with αl = 1 and Wup = 0, so that the teacher equals the student at initialization. Together, the two modules contain about 13M parameters. Optimization. All stages use AdamW [31] with β = (0.9, 0.95), weight decay of 0.01, cosine schedule with 5% linear warm-up, and gradient clipping at 1.0. Training runs in bfloat16 with DeepSpeed ZeRO-2 [37] on 8 GPUs with 24 GB of memory each, using seed 42. The video expert is frozen in every stage of every method except full SFT. Tab. 3 lists the stage-specific settings. In Stage 0, we use λBC = 2, which matches the total gradient scale of the distillation stage (λdist + λBC = 2). In Stage B, the energy score uses = 4 student samples, = 1 supervised point, and one teacher sample, with λdist = λBC = 1. At inference, only the student is used, conditioned on the current frame, the instruction, and the proprioceptive state; on LIBERO, it replans every 10 control steps. On RoboTwin, all hyperparameters are reused from LIBERO without any tuning. Baselines. The BC control and full SFT use the same data, optimizer, schedule, and effective batch size as HINTWAM (Tab. 3). The BC control is Stage with the distillation term removed (λdist = 0, λBC = 1): it starts from SFT at step 3,000 and trains the action expert for 2,000 further steps with the flow-matching loss of Eq. (1), so it matches HINT-WAM in initialization, trainable parameters, and number of steps but has no teacher. Full SFT follows Stage 0 (λBC = 2, 5,000 steps from the released checkpoint), but trains both the video and the action expert (6.02B parameters); we report its final checkpoint. On RoboTwin, the BC control, full SFT, and HINT-WAM all start from the released RoboTwin checkpoint and train for 2,000 steps. B. Training Cost We measure the training time on 8 GPUs with 24 GB of memory from checkpoint timestamps, so the reported times include periodic evaluation and checkpoint saving. GPUhours are computed as steps seconds per step 8/3600. Tab. 4 lists the cost of every stage and pipeline on LIBERO90. HINT-WAM, consisting of SFT for 3,000 steps followed by Stages and B, costs 1.28 the 5,000-step SFT pipeline and 0.56 full SFT. full-SFT step costs 2.3 an actionexpert step (91.4 vs. 40.2 s) because the 5B-parameter video expert is also trained. Inference is unchanged: the deployed student is the unmodified Fast-WAM with 10 Euler steps, and the teacher and the hindsight encoder are discarded after training. On RoboTwin, Stage takes 18.1 per step (80 GPU-hours for 2,000 steps), Stage 60.6 (269 GPU-hours), and the BC control 37.8 (168 GPUhours). C. Hindsight Teacher Checks Before Stage B, we verify that hindsight lowers the teachers flow-matching loss on held-out frames, using 200 held-out batches and paired comparison of the teacher with and without ϕ. Tab. 5 shows that hindsight reduces the action loss of every teacher, and that the advantage of the LIBERO-90 teacher keeps growing from 1,000 to 2,000 training steps. The teacher must be built on the model being distilled. In 20-task pilot with 10 trials per task, teacher built on the weaker released checkpoint instead of the SFT model pulled the student down from 55.0% to 47.5%, below SFT 3.28% (t = 5.77) LIBERO-90, built on SFT LIBERO-90 + replay, built on SFT + replay 3.06% (t = 4.68) RoboTwin 2.0, built on released checkpoint 5.37% (t = 3.43) 2.36% 3.28% LIBERO-90, 1,000 vs. 2,000 steps (with the velocity-matching objective). This supports the design choice in Sec. 3.3 that the teacher shares the students initialization θ0. D. Full Paired Statistics on LIBERO-90 All tests are paired over the 90 LIBERO-90 tasks with 50 trials each. For every comparison, Tab. 6 reports the mean difference in success rate, its standard error, the paired tstatistic, the numbers of tasks on which the first method wins, loses, or ties, and the exact two-sided sign test over the non-tied tasks. The standard error for shuffled hindsight is derived from its mean difference and t-statistic. All LIBERO-90 numbers in the paper, including the released Fast-WAM and the BC control, use 50 trials per task. SFT reaches 78.88% at both step 3,000 and step 5,000. E. Per-Task Analysis Fig. 8 shows how the gain is distributed over the 90 tasks. HINT-WAM improves 36 tasks, leaves 32 unchanged, and lowers 22. The gain is concentrated on the tasks where SFT is weak: +32.2% on the 13 tasks where SFT succeeds less than half of the time and +11.5% on the 15 tasks between 50% and 80%. On the 42 tasks that SFT already solves ( 95%), the change is small (1.7%, i.e., less than one failed episode out of 50). The many ties and small losses on saturated tasks explain why the sign test is weaker than the paired t-test (Tab. 6). Since tasks are grouped by the success rate of SFT itself, part of this trend may reflect regression to the mean. Table 6. Paired statistics on LIBERO-90. Tab. 7 lists the tasks with the largest drops for three pairs of methods. Most drops of HINT-WAM relative to SFT occur on pick-andplace tasks into basket or caddy compartment. Task 74 (pick up the book and place it in the left compartment of the caddy) is hurt by both distillation objectives, but much more by velocity matching (80% 32%) than by the energy score (80% 60%). Task instructions: 5, put the chocolate pudding in the top drawer of the cabinet and close it; 52, pick up the milk and put it in the basket; 53, pick up the orange juice and put it in the basket; 74, pick up the book and place it in the left compartment of the caddy; 78, pick up the task before any of our Hard subset. We keep the 25 tasks on which scores below 95% in eireleased checkpoint the the randomized setting, measured ther the clean or with 20 episodes per trainblocks ranking size, handover block, ing: move stapler pad, move can pot, open microwave, hanging mug, pick diverse bottles, place a2b left, place bread basket, place a2b right, place can basket, place bread skillet, place dual shoes, place mouse pad, place object basket, place object scale, put bottles dustbin, place object stand, rotate qrcode, put object cabinet, stack blocks three, scan object, stack bowls three, stamp seal, and turn switch. Evaluation uses 50 episodes per task and setting. All methods start from the released checkpoint with the same data, 2,000 steps, learning rate of 104, and batch size of 192. Paired tests. Tab. 8 reports paired tests over the 25 tasks. HINT-WAM improves over the BC control in both settings, with borderline significance in the clean setting, while its difference from the released checkpoint is not significant. Continued full SFT also lowers success, by 2.36% in the clean and 0.20% in the randomized setting, and HINTWAM exceeds it by 2.92 and 0.44%, respectively. Since the released checkpoint was already trained on this data, little headroom remains: continued training lowers success, whether by BC or by full fine-tuning, whereas HINT-WAM keeps it at or slightly above the level of the released checkpoint. G. Evaluation Protocol on LIBERO-90 Training and evaluation use the same 90 tasks but not the same episodes. Training uses the recorded human demonstrations (3,921 episodes, 569K frames), of which 10% (393 episodes, split once with fixed seed) are excluded from training and used only for offline loss metrics. Evaluation runs 50 new closed-loop episodes per task from the fixed initial states provided by LIBERO, which are generated separately from the demonstrations. This is the standard LIBERO protocol, also used by OpenVLA [18], π0 [5], and Fast-WAM [45]. We find no sign that the test placements are memorized: the SFT checkpoint at step 3,000 reaches 80.94% on 1,800 random placements, which never coincide with the test placements, and 78.88% on the fixed test placements. Our evaluation thus measures generalization to held-out initial configurations of the training tasks rather than to unseen tasks. H. Self-Imitation Baseline The SFT checkpoint at step 3,000 was rolled out from 20 random initial placements per task, none of which coincides with the test placements, yielding 1,800 episodes, of which 1,457 (80.94%) succeeded. We added 1,454 successful episodes (203K frames, about 26% of the training frames) to the LIBERO-90 demonstrations, excluding three episodes whose instruction does not appear in the training data. Training then followed Stage of HINT-WAM with the behavior-cloning loss only, starting from SFT step 3,000 for 2,000 steps with learning rate of 104 and batch size of 192. I. Selection of the Objective and Learning Rate Most hyperparameters are inherited from Fast-WAM or fixed by design, and the loss weights, adapter placement, and hindsight size were not tuned. The few design decisions we made were based on the held-out LIBERO-90 episodes and 20-task pilot on LIBERO-90 with 10 trials per task; no tuning was performed on RoboTwin. Learning rate. An initial round with learning rate of 105 for 500 steps left every method under-trained, at or below 16% on LIBERO-90. We therefore used 104, the fine-tuning learning rate of Fast-WAM. Objective. On the held-out episodes, the energy score reduced the error of the generated actions more than velocity matching (23.7% vs. 15.5% relative to the baseline). The closed-loop results confirm this choice (85.18% vs. 79.02%, Tab. 6). Supervised points. With the 2 weighting on our 10step schedule, the last point carries 63.6% of the mass and the last three points 91.1%. We therefore use = 1 for the energy score and = 3 for velocity matching. With = 1, the selected point is σN , so the implied action ˆam,1 is exactly the output of the m-th student rollout. J. Toy Experiment: Mode Averaging The toy example in Fig. 9 isolates the mode-averaging effect of velocity matching. hidden binary variable decides which of two actions is correct; the teacher observes it, and the student does not. Distilled with the squared error, the student predicts the average of the two actions, which lands on neither mode (success 0.00). Distilled with the energy score from the same single teacher samples and = 4, it places its samples on both modes (success 0.92). The same mechanism explains why velocity matching yields no gain on LIBERO-90, while the energy score improves success by 6.16% over it (Tab. 6). Setup. The observation is U(1, 1), and hidden {1, +1}, drawn independently of with equal probability, sets the correct action = (1+0.5x), so the student cannot infer and no single action is correct for both values. The teacher observes and outputs the correct action, and each training state provides one teacher sample. The student is an implicit sampler = (x, z) with (0, 1), implemented as an MLP with two hidden layers of 64 units and GELU activations. Both students are trained for 3,000 steps with Adam (learning rate 3 103, batch size 256): the squared-error student regresses one sample onto the teacher sample, and the energy-score student matches = 4 samples to it. Success is the fraction of student samples within 0.25 of either correct action, computed over 64 values of with 512 samples each and averaged over 3 seeds; student that predicts the mean of the two actions therefore scores zero. K. Qualitative Rollouts Figs. 10 to 12 show closed-loop rollouts in which HINTWAM succeeds where the baseline fails. Each pair of rows starts from the same initial state; the frames are evenly Table 8. Paired tests on the RoboTwin 2.0 hard subset. Mean difference in % (SE, t) and wins / losses / ties over 25 tasks. (b) Squared-error distillation collapses to the mean of the two modes. (c) The energy score recovers both. spaced over the episode, and the badge on the last frame marks success or failure. New tasks. Fig. 11 shows four LIBERO-90 tasks. The failures of SFT are typically errors in the final stage of the task rather than in grasping: the moka pot is not set down on the stove (task 19), the drawer is left open after the butter has been placed (task 3), the bowl is not placed on the cabinet (task 43), and the book is dropped into the wrong compartment of the caddy (task 81). HINT-WAM completes each of these tasks from the same initial state. Retained skills. Fig. 12 shows tasks from the original LIBERO suites, which the released Fast-WAM solves before post-training. After post-training on LIBERO-90 without replay, SFT fails these tasks, whereas HINT-WAM still solves them, consistent with its smaller forgetting in Tab. 2. four RoboTwin 2.0. Fig. 10 shows episodes of stack bowls three (clean setting). SFT moves single bowls but never completes the stack: it carries bowl without placing it (a), loses track of the remaining bowls (b), flips bowl (c), or stops after one lift (d), whereas HINT-WAM stacks all three. Both reach the same success rate on this task, so these episodes illustrate failure modes rather than per-task gain. L. Discussion Why does teacher that sees the future help? The student never receives ϕ; the teacher supplies one action sample per state. Since the energy score is strictly proper, the student is driven towards the distribution of teacher actions given what it observes, i.e., the continuations consistent with the demonstrations, not one particular future. Hindsight thus resolves the ambiguity of the SFT target rather than giving information the student must recover. The gain requires the correct future: with the future of another episode, the same pipeline reaches only 80.28% (Tab. 1). In what sense is HINT-WAM on-policy? The states are on-policy with respect to the action sampler: the student is supervised on the denoising states its own ODE visits; noised demonstrations instead reach only 80.74%  (Fig. 7)  . The observations still come from the demonstrations, so HINT-WAM needs neither rewards nor simulator, but does not address compounding errors across control steps and is complementary to DAgger or reinforcement learning. Is the gain due to extra compute or tuning? No. The same 2,000 extra steps without the teacher lower success to 71.56%, and HINT-WAM exceeds full SFT by 3.94% at 0.56 its cost (Tab. 4).
